item.title: MB 1. Nucleic acid chemistry
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
MB(ASCP) study notes · Lesson 1

DNA and RNA are polymers. The exam mostly asks you to name the parts, the bonds, and the one chemical difference that makes RNA fall apart in alkali. This lesson is that map.

NoteScope

Original study notes for MB(ASCP) and MB(ASCPi) preparation. Not an official ASCP publication, not a dosing or lab procedure, and not a set of real examination items. Confirm the current content outline before you register.

Three pieces, two names

Every nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar, and at least one phosphate. The sugar–phosphate chain is the backbone. The order of the bases is the information.

Molecule What it contains Examples
Base The ring only Adenine, guanine, cytosine, thymine, uracil
Nucleoside Base + sugar Adenosine, deoxyadenosine, thymidine, uridine
Nucleotide Base + sugar + phosphate AMP, ATP, dATP, dTTP

The base is tied to carbon 1′ of the sugar by a glycosidic bond. Purines use nitrogen N9. Pyrimidines use nitrogen N1. The phosphate sits on carbon 5′. The next nucleotide will be attached to the free OH on carbon 3′.

Original study schematic. Carbon numbers, not artistic ring drawings, are what the items test.

Naming is part of the question. Adenine is the base, adenosine is the ribonucleoside, and AMP is the nucleotide. The prefix deoxy- means the sugar is 2′-deoxyribose, so dATP is a DNA building block. Thymidine is the usual name for the deoxyribonucleoside of thymine. Uridine is the ribonucleoside of uracil.

Purines and pyrimidines

Purines have two fused rings. Pyrimidines have one ring.

Purines Pyrimidines
Shape Six-membered ring fused to a five-membered ring One six-membered ring
Members Adenine (A), guanine (G) Cytosine (C), thymine (T), uracil (U)
Where A and G are in DNA and RNA C is in both. T is the DNA base. U is the RNA base.

The memory line is enough: purines are A and G (“pure As gold”). Everything else in this family — C, T, and U — is a pyrimidine.

A few substituents are worth being able to picture. Adenine carries an amino group. Guanine carries an amino group and a carbonyl. Thymine is uracil with a methyl group on carbon 5, which is why thymine is also called 5-methyluracil. That methyl group is the only difference the exam wants between T and U.

If the item shows rings and asks which atom bonds to the sugar Count the rings first. Two rings means a purine, and the glycosidic nitrogen is N9. One ring means a pyrimidine, and the glycosidic nitrogen is N1. A choice that swaps those two numbers is the usual distractor.

DNA and RNA

DNA RNA
Sugar 2′-deoxyribose (2′ carbon carries H) Ribose (2′ carbon carries OH)
Bases A, G, C, T A, G, C, U
Usual form Double-stranded Single-stranded, often folded
Alkali The backbone resists this particular attack The 2′-OH can cleave the backbone

The 2′-OH is the whole stability story the board wants. Under alkaline conditions that hydroxyl can attack the neighboring phosphate and cut the chain. DNA has no 2′-OH, so it does not have this path. Folding, proteins, and RNases still decide how long an RNA actually lasts in a tube. The chemical point remains: RNA is the alkali-labile nucleic acid because of the 2′-OH.

DNA polymerases are given dNTPs. RNA polymerases are given NTPs. ATP is both an energy cofactor and an RNA building block. If a stem says “the polymerase incorporates ATP,” check whether the product is RNA before you call it a trick.

Two bonds, and which direction the strands run

Hydrogen bonds pair bases across the two strands. A phosphodiester bond links nucleotides along one strand, from the 3′ carbon of one sugar to the 5′ phosphate of the next.

Pair Hydrogen bonds Where you meet it
A–T 2 DNA
A–U 2 RNA duplexes and DNA–RNA hybrids
G–C 3 DNA and RNA

G–C is the stronger pair because it has three hydrogen bonds. Base stacking along the strand stabilizes the duplex as well. The exam still treats “three versus two” as the short answer.

The strands of a duplex are antiparallel. One runs 5′→3′. Its partner runs 3′→5′. Sequence is written 5′ to 3′ unless the item says otherwise.

In double-stranded DNA, Chargaff’s rules follow from that pairing: the amount of A equals T, and the amount of G equals C. A single strand does not have to obey that equality. An item that applies Chargaff to one RNA strand is using the rule in the wrong place.

Hydrogen bonds are the cross-links. Phosphodiester bonds are the rails. Antiparallel means the 5′ ends are at opposite corners.

Melting temperature

Tm is the temperature at which half of the duplexes in a population are denatured, under the conditions you actually used. As the strands separate, absorbance at 260 nm rises. That rise is the hyperchromic effect, and it is how a melting curve is read.

What pushes Tm up, when the other variables stay put:

  • More G–C pairs, because each contributes three hydrogen bonds and favorable stacking.
  • A longer perfectly matched duplex.
  • Higher salt. Monovalent cations shield the repulsion between the phosphate backbones.

What pushes Tm down:

  • Mismatches.
  • A shorter duplex.
  • Denaturants such as formamide or urea, which is why hybridization buffers use them when the goal is a more stringent, or a more controlled, melt.

GC percent is a first estimate. Primer-design software uses nearest-neighbor parameters, because the neighbors of a pair change the stability of that pair. Two oligos with the same GC percent can still have different Tm values. For a board item that only gives GC percent, length, and “otherwise identical conditions,” choose the higher GC.

In the lab this shows up as soon as you set an annealing temperature. Primers that melt far apart, or an annealing step set far below the primer Tm, are the usual reasons a PCR becomes either weak or nonspecific. The chemistry lesson and the amplification lesson are the same fact seen from two sides.

Say these without looking

  • Purines: A and G, two rings, glycosidic bond through N9.
  • Pyrimidines: C, T, and U, one ring, glycosidic bond through N1.
  • Nucleoside = base + sugar. Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate.
  • DNA sugar is 2′-deoxyribose and the unique base is T. RNA sugar is ribose and the unique base is U.
  • The 2′-OH makes RNA alkali-labile.
  • A–T and A–U have two hydrogen bonds. G–C has three.
  • Phosphodiester bonds run along a strand. Hydrogen bonds pair the strands. The strands are antiparallel.
  • Tm is 50% denaturation. Higher GC, greater length, and higher salt raise it. Mismatches and formamide lower it.

Next: DNA replication.

Check yourself

Ten original questions. Answer all of them, then check. A miss opens a one-line reason.

1. Which bases are purines?

Adenine and guanine have two fused rings. C, T, and U are the pyrimidines.

2. A nucleoside contains which parts?

Base plus sugar is the nucleoside. Phosphate is what turns it into a nucleotide. dATP is a nucleotide, not a nucleoside.

3. Which bond covalently links neighboring nucleotides in one strand?

The phosphodiester bond is the backbone link, from 3′ of one sugar to 5′ of the next. Hydrogen bonds pair bases. The glycosidic bond holds a base on its own sugar.

4. Why is RNA more susceptible than DNA to alkaline hydrolysis?

The 2′-OH can attack the adjacent phosphate and cut the chain. DNA carries hydrogen at the 2′ carbon, so this path does not exist.

5. How many hydrogen bonds hold a G–C pair?

G–C has three hydrogen bonds. A–T and A–U have two. The bonds are not covalent.

6. Which duplex should have the highest Tm?

Length and GC content both raise Tm. Mismatches lower it. The long matched 70% GC duplex has all three factors on its side.

7. A purine is attached to C1′ of the sugar through which atom?

Purines use N9. Pyrimidines use N1. Both bonds land on C1′ of the sugar.

8. Chargaff's rules, A = T and G = C, apply directly to which molecule?

The equalities come from base pairing across two DNA strands. A single RNA strand has no partner forcing A to equal U.

9. What does Tm represent?

Tm is the midpoint of the melting transition under stated conditions: 50% of the duplex population is single-stranded. It is measured, often from the rise in A260, not assumed from a reagent label.

10. Which change tends to lower Tm?

Formamide destabilizes the duplex and lowers Tm. GC content, salt, and length of a matched duplex move Tm the other way.

Where this sits

Figures on this page are original schematics. The chemistry is the standard account used for clinical molecular boards: nucleotide structure, pairing, and melting behavior as treated in Alberts and colleagues, Molecular Biology of the Cell, and in the nucleic-acid chapters of Buckingham, Molecular Diagnostics. Use the current ASCP Board of Certification content guideline for MB(ASCP) and MB(ASCPi) to decide what else is in scope for your sitting.

item.title: MB 2. DNA replication
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
MB(ASCP) study notes · Lesson 2

Replication makes two duplexes from one, and each daughter duplex keeps one old strand. Almost every exam item after that sentence is a direction, an enzyme, or a strand assignment. Learn those three lists and the questions get short.

NoteScope

Original study notes for MB(ASCP) and MB(ASCPi) preparation. Not an official ASCP publication and not real examination items.

One old strand, one new strand

Replication is semiconservative. The parental strands separate, and each is the template for a new partner. Each daughter duplex therefore contains one parental strand and one new strand.

Meselson and Stahl showed this in E. coli by labeling DNA with heavy nitrogen (15N) and then shifting the cells to light nitrogen (14N). After exactly one generation in light medium, the DNA formed a single band of intermediate density. After exactly two generations, half of the DNA was intermediate and half was light. A conservative model would have kept a fully heavy duplex and made a fully light one. The two-generation result is the one that separates semiconservative copying from the alternatives.

Who stands at the fork

Protein Job at the fork
Helicase Pulls the strands apart. It disrupts base pairs. It does not cut the backbone.
Single-strand binding protein Coats the separated DNA so the strands do not simply zip back together.
Topoisomerase Cuts and reseals DNA ahead of the fork so the unreplicated duplex does not overwind. Bacterial DNA gyrase is a type II topoisomerase.
Primase Lays down a short RNA primer. DNA polymerase cannot start a chain.
DNA polymerase Adds nucleotides to a free 3′-OH. Synthesis is 5′→3′.
Sliding clamp Holds the polymerase on the DNA. The bacterial clamp is the β clamp. The eukaryotic clamp is PCNA.
Ligase Seals a nick by making the missing phosphodiester bond. E. coli ligase uses NAD+. Eukaryotic ligase and T4 ligase use ATP.

Helicase versus topoisomerase is a standard pair of distractors. Helicase separates strands. Topoisomerase manages the twist in front of that separation. Ligase is the enzyme of the nick, not the enzyme of the primer.

Direction, primers, and the two new strands

DNA polymerase reads the template 3′→5′ and writes the new strand 5′→3′. It can add a nucleotide only onto a free 3′-OH. That is why a primer exists. In the cell the primer is RNA, made by primase. In PCR the primer is a synthetic DNA oligo, and heat does the unwinding that helicase does in the cell.

The two templates are antiparallel, and the polymerase still writes only 5′→3′. One new strand can grow continuously toward the moving fork. That is the leading strand. The other new strand is made as short pieces, Okazaki fragments, each of them still 5′→3′ and pointed away from the fork. That is the lagging strand. A common miss is to say the lagging strand is polymerized 3′→5′. It is not. The fragments face the other way, and ligase joins them later.

The newest Okazaki fragment is the short one nearest the fork. Its primer has not been removed yet.

Approximate fragment length, the range items expect:

Organism Okazaki fragments
Bacteria such as E. coli About 1,000–2,000 nucleotides
Eukaryotes About 100–200 nucleotides

Maturation is the same story in both kingdoms, with different enzymes. Primase makes the RNA primer. Polymerase extends it. The RNA is removed and the gap is filled with DNA. Ligase seals the last nick. In E. coli, DNA polymerase I removes the primer with its 5′→3′ exonuclease and fills the gap. In eukaryotes, RNase H and FEN1 do the removal work, polymerase fills, and ligase seals.

Which polymerase, on an exam

Bacterial assignments:

Enzyme What to answer
DNA polymerase III The main chromosomal replicase.
DNA polymerase I Removes RNA primers and fills the gaps. Also works in repair. It has 5′→3′ polymerase, 3′→5′ proofreading, and 5′→3′ exonuclease.
DNA polymerase II Repair and restart. Not the main replicase.

Eukaryotic assignments used on exams:

Enzyme What to answer
DNA polymerase α Works with primase. Makes the RNA–DNA starter.
DNA polymerase ε Leading strand.
DNA polymerase δ Lagging strand.
DNA polymerase γ Mitochondrial DNA.

In the cell these enzymes share a replisome, and the labor is a little more shared than a one-enzyme-one-strand sentence suggests. For the item in front of you, use the table. Pol α starts the chain. Pol ε leads. Pol δ lags. Pol γ is the mitochondrial enzyme. A choice that makes Pol α the enzyme that finishes the chromosome is swapping the starter for the replicase.

Proofreading is a direction

Replicative polymerases check the base they just added. If it is wrong, a 3′→5′ exonuclease cuts it back off and synthesis continues. That activity is proofreading. Mismatch repair is a later, separate system. It is not the same activity.

Activity Direction What it is for
Synthesis 5′→3′ Adding the next nucleotide
Proofreading 3′→5′ exonuclease Removing a base the polymerase just misincorporated
Primer removal by E. coli Pol I 5′→3′ exonuclease Clearing RNA in front of the filling polymerase

The trap is to swap the two exonuclease directions. Proofreading walks backward on the new strand. Primer removal chews forward from the 5′ side of the RNA.

The ends of a linear chromosome

Bacterial chromosomes are circular, so the fork can finish. Eukaryotic chromosomes are linear. On the lagging strand, removing the terminal RNA primer leaves a gap, and no polymerase can fill it, because there is no upstream 3′-OH to extend. That is the end-replication problem.

Telomerase solves the shortening. It is a reverse transcriptase that carries its own RNA template and extends the 3′ overhang with telomere repeats. Ordinary DNA synthesis then fills part of the complementary strand. The overhang remains, and it is part of how the end is protected. If an item says “RNA-dependent DNA polymerase at the chromosome end,” the enzyme is telomerase.

The same rules, inside a PCR tube

Step Typical temperature What replaces the cell
Denaturation 94–98°C Heat replaces helicase
Annealing Often 50–65°C, set from the primer Tm Synthetic DNA primers replace RNA primers
Extension About 72°C with Taq A thermostable polymerase replaces Pol III

Taq polymerase, from Thermus aquaticus, survives the denaturation step. Conventional Taq has little 3′→5′ proofreading, so the copied product accumulates errors. When the goal is a low error rate — cloning, for example — the reaction uses a high-fidelity polymerase that does proofread. Taq also tends to leave a single unpaired A on the 3′ end of the product. That overhang is a cloning detail, and it is fair game on a techniques item.

Say these without looking

  • Replication is semiconservative. After two generations in light nitrogen, expect half intermediate and half light DNA.
  • Helicase unwinds. Topoisomerase relieves twist ahead of the fork. Primase makes RNA primers. Ligase seals nicks.
  • Polymerase writes 5′→3′ and can start only from a 3′-OH.
  • Leading strand: one continuous chain toward the fork. Lagging strand: Okazaki fragments, each still 5′→3′.
  • E. coli Pol III replicates the chromosome. Pol I removes primers with a 5′→3′ exonuclease.
  • Exam assignment: Pol α starts, Pol ε leads, Pol δ lags, Pol γ replicates mitochondrial DNA.
  • Proofreading is 3′→5′. Primer removal by Pol I is 5′→3′.
  • PCR uses heat and DNA primers. Taq does not proofread well.

Previous: Nucleic acid chemistry. Next: Transcription and RNA processing.

Check yourself

1. Cells grown for many generations in heavy nitrogen are switched to light nitrogen. After exactly two generations, semiconservative replication predicts which DNA?

Each daughter keeps one old strand. After two generations, half the duplexes are heavy–light and half are fully light. A heavy band plus a light band would have supported conservative copying.

2. Which enzyme separates the parental strands without cutting the phosphodiester backbone?

Helicase breaks base pairs. Topoisomerase is the enzyme that cuts the backbone, and it does so ahead of the fork to relieve twist, then reseals it.

3. DNA polymerase can add the next nucleotide only to which chemical group?

Synthesis is extension of a 3′ end, which is why a primer is required and why the chain grows 5′→3′.

4. Why is lagging-strand synthesis discontinuous?

Both new strands are made 5′→3′. One template faces the fork, so its new strand is continuous. The other template faces the other way, so its new strand is made in Okazaki fragments.

5. Which enzyme is the main replicase of the E. coli chromosome?

Pol III copies the chromosome. Pol I removes RNA primers and fills short gaps. Pol γ is the eukaryotic mitochondrial polymerase, not a bacterial enzyme.

6. In E. coli, RNA primers are removed by which activity?

Pol I uses a 5′→3′ exonuclease to clear the RNA primer, then fills with DNA. The 3′→5′ exonuclease is proofreading, a different job.

7. Proofreading by a replicative DNA polymerase is which activity?

Proofreading removes a nucleotide that was just added, so the nuclease moves 3′→5′ on the new strand. Primer removal runs the other direction.

8. On the standard exam assignment, which eukaryotic polymerase synthesizes the leading strand?

Pol ε is the leading-strand enzyme. Pol δ is assigned to the lagging strand. Pol α starts synthesis with primase. Pol γ replicates mitochondrial DNA.

9. Mitochondrial DNA is replicated by which polymerase?

Pol γ is the mitochondrial replicase. Nuclear leading and lagging strands are Pol ε and Pol δ.

10. Conventional Taq polymerase is a poor choice when the copied sequence must have the lowest possible error rate because it

Taq survives heat denaturation but does not proofread well. A high-fidelity polymerase is used when the error rate matters. Taq still extends DNA primers 5′→3′.

Where this sits

The fork drawing is an original schematic. Strand assignments for the eukaryotic polymerases follow the account used in exams and in standard texts (Pol ε on the leading strand, Pol δ on the lagging strand), with the caveat that the replisome in vivo is more cooperative than the table. Telomerase as an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase at chromosome ends is the same textbook account, as in Alberts and colleagues, Molecular Biology of the Cell. PCR enzyme behavior is the clinical-lab version of those rules, as taught in Buckingham, Molecular Diagnostics.

item.title: MB 3. Transcription and RNA processing
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
MB(ASCP) study notes · Lesson 3

Transcription copies DNA into RNA. The exam then asks which strand was read, which polymerase did the job, and what eukaryotes do to a pre-mRNA before it can be translated. Processing is three events: a 5′ cap, splicing, and a poly-A tail.

NoteScope

Original study notes for MB(ASCP) and MB(ASCPi) preparation. Not an official ASCP publication and not real examination items.

What the polymerase reads

RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3′→5′ and writes RNA 5′→3′. It does not need a primer. The new RNA uses uracil where DNA would have used thymine.

The other DNA strand is the coding strand, also called the sense strand. Its sequence matches the RNA, with T standing where the RNA has U. The polymerase does not copy the coding strand. People get this backward because the coding strand “looks like” the product. It looks like the product because the template was its complement.

Read a short example as a habit:

Sequence
Coding DNA 5′-ATG CCA TTT-3′
Template DNA 3′-TAC GGT AAA-5′
RNA 5′-AUG CCA UUU-3′

The RNA is complementary to the template and identical to the coding strand except at U. If an item gives you the template and asks for the RNA, write the complement and flip the direction so the answer runs 5′→3′.

Template equals antisense. Coding equals sense. Report both sequences 5′ to 3′ unless the question prints the template in the 3′→5′ direction it is read.

Three stages, and where bacteria and eukaryotes differ

Stage What happens
Initiation Polymerase and its helper proteins find a promoter and start at the +1 nucleotide.
Elongation The polymerase walks the template and lengthens the RNA 5′→3′.
Termination A signal ends the transcript. The signal is not the same in bacteria and eukaryotes.

A promoter decides where transcription starts and how eager the start is. It is DNA. It is not transcribed into the body of a bacterial mRNA as a coding sequence, and it is not the same thing as the start codon.

In bacteria the core RNA polymerase is α2ββ′ω. The sigma subunit is what recognizes the promoter, principally the −10 box (TATAAT) and the −35 box (TTGACA). Sigma leaves after initiation. The core enzyme elongates without it.

Bacterial termination comes in two versions. Intrinsic, or rho-independent, termination is an RNA hairpin rich in G–C, followed by a run of U. The weak A–U hybrid lets the chain fall off. Rho-dependent termination uses the rho protein, which loads on a C-rich rut site in the RNA and catches the polymerase.

Eukaryotes split the work among three nuclear polymerases:

Polymerase What to answer
RNA polymerase I The major ribosomal RNAs: 28S, 18S, and 5.8S, cut from one precursor
RNA polymerase II Pre-mRNA, and also most snRNA and miRNA
RNA polymerase III tRNA, 5S rRNA, and U6 snRNA

The memory line is Pol I for most rRNA, Pol II for pre-mRNA, Pol III for tRNA and 5S. The item that catches people is 5S rRNA. It is ribosomal, but it is a Pol III product. U6 is the snRNA exception in the other direction: most snRNAs are Pol II, and U6 is Pol III.

Eukaryotic promoters are more varied. Many Pol II promoters have a TATA box near −25, recognized by TBP within TFIID. Others rely on an initiator, a CAAT box, or GC boxes. “Every eukaryotic gene has a TATA box” is false.

The RNA types worth naming

RNA Job
mRNA Carries codons to the ribosome
tRNA Brings the amino acid. Its anticodon pairs with the codon.
rRNA Builds the ribosome and takes part in peptide-bond formation
snRNA Works inside snRNPs during splicing
miRNA and siRNA Short RNAs that regulate other RNAs
lncRNA Long noncoding RNAs with regulatory roles

You do not need a catalog of every lncRNA. You need to know that a transcript can be functional without becoming a protein, and that mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA are three different answers.

What happens to eukaryotic pre-mRNA

Bacteria often translate an mRNA while it is still being made, and a bacterial mRNA does not receive a 5′ cap or a long poly-A tail of the eukaryotic kind. Eukaryotic protein-coding genes produce a pre-mRNA that is processed, mostly while polymerase II is still elongating. Phosphorylation of the Pol II C-terminal domain is what couples the polymerase to the processing machinery. The three events are the cap, splicing, and cleavage plus polyadenylation.

Original schematic. Introns leave. The poly-A tail is added by an enzyme after the RNA is cut downstream of AAUAAA.

The cap

A 7-methylguanosine is attached to the 5′ end through an unusual 5′–5′ triphosphate bridge. The cap protects the mRNA from exonucleases, helps export it from the nucleus, and helps the ribosome find the message. It is added early, co-transcriptionally.

The tail

A polyadenylation signal, commonly AAUAAA in mammals, sits near the 3′ end of the pre-mRNA. The transcript is cleaved downstream of that signal. Poly-A polymerase then adds a string of adenines to the new 3′ end. Those adenines are not copied from a long run of T in the gene. The tail contributes to stability, export, and translation. A shorter tail is one way a cell retires an mRNA.

Splicing

Introns are removed. Exons are joined and stay in the mature mRNA. Many nuclear pre-mRNA introns begin with GU and end with AG. An adenine at the branch point, upstream of the 3′ splice site, attacks the 5′ splice site. The intron comes out as a lariat, and the exons are ligated.

The spliceosome is the RNA–protein machine that does this. Its snRNPs include U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6. U1 recognizes the 5′ splice site. U2 recognizes the branch point. The chemistry itself is RNA-catalyzed. A few introns, the group I and group II types, can splice without a spliceosome. If the stem says “spliceosome,” it means the GU–AG nuclear pre-mRNA pathway, not those self-splicing exceptions.

Word Meaning on an item
Exon Kept in the mature RNA
Intron Removed
Spliceosome The complex that removes nuclear pre-mRNA introns
snRNP An RNA–protein subunit of that complex

Alternative splicing lets one gene produce more than one mature mRNA. A transcript with exons 1–2–3–4 might be processed as 1–2–4 or as 1–3–4. Exon skipping is the common human pattern. Other patterns are an alternative 5′ or 3′ splice site, mutually exclusive exons, and intron retention. The result is more than one protein, or a different untranslated region, from one locus. A splicing mutation can cause disease without changing a single codon inside an exon. RNA sequencing is one way a lab sees the abnormal junction.

Reverse transcription, said so the abbreviations stop colliding

Process Direction Primer? Enzyme
Replication DNA → DNA Yes DNA polymerase
Transcription DNA → RNA No RNA polymerase
Reverse transcription RNA → DNA Yes Reverse transcriptase

Reverse transcriptase reads RNA 3′→5′ and writes DNA 5′→3′. Unlike RNA polymerase, it needs a primer. For mRNA the primer is often oligo(dT), which pairs with the poly-A tail. Random primers are used when the RNA has no tail, or when the goal is to copy more than the 3′ end. Retroviral reverse transcriptase also has an RNase H activity that degrades the RNA half of the hybrid.

In the clinical lab:

  • PCR starts from DNA.
  • RT-PCR starts from RNA, makes complementary DNA with reverse transcriptase, and then runs PCR.
  • qPCR, or real-time PCR, is a way of watching product accumulate, with a dye or a probe. It says nothing by itself about whether the input was RNA.
  • RT-qPCR is both: reverse transcription, then real-time detection.

“RT” in a method name is the abbreviation that causes the miss. On these notes, RT means reverse transcription. Real-time is written out, or written as qPCR.

Say these without looking

  • RNA polymerase reads the template 3′→5′ and writes 5′→3′. It does not need a primer.
  • The coding strand matches the RNA, with T where RNA has U.
  • Bacteria: sigma reads −10 and −35. Intrinsic termination is a hairpin plus a U run. Rho termination uses the rho protein.
  • Pol I: 28S, 18S, 5.8S. Pol II: pre-mRNA. Pol III: tRNA, 5S rRNA, U6.
  • The cap is 7-methylguanosine on a 5′–5′ link.
  • AAUAAA is the common polyadenylation signal. The tail is added, not transcribed.
  • Introns leave through the spliceosome. GU–AG and a branch-point adenine define the usual nuclear intron. Exons stay.
  • Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA and needs a primer. RT-PCR is that step plus PCR. qPCR is the detection format.

Previous: DNA replication. The usual next block after these three days is translation and the genetic code. That lesson is not on the site yet.

Check yourself

1. Which strand does RNA polymerase read, and in which direction?

The template, or antisense, strand is read 3′→5′. The coding strand matches the RNA and is not the template.

2. How does a mature mRNA sequence compare with the coding strand of its gene?

Coding-strand sequence and RNA sequence are the same letters, with U replacing T, and with introns already removed from the mature mRNA.

3. Which eukaryotic polymerase synthesizes pre-mRNA?

Pol II makes pre-mRNA. Pol I makes the major rRNAs. Pol III makes tRNA, 5S rRNA, and U6.

4. tRNA and 5S rRNA are products of which polymerase?

Both are Pol III products. 5S is the ribosomal RNA that does not come from Pol I. The other rRNAs, 28S, 18S, and 5.8S, do.

5. The 5′ cap on eukaryotic mRNA is which structure?

The cap is a modified guanine on an unusual 5′–5′ triphosphate bridge. RNA polymerase does not use a primer, and the poly-A tail is a separate 3′ modification.

6. Which sequence is the common mammalian polyadenylation signal?

AAUAAA marks the cleavage and polyadenylation region. TATAAT and TTGACA are bacterial promoter boxes. GU–AG marks splice sites.

7. During splicing of a typical nuclear pre-mRNA intron, the branch-point adenine

The branch-point A makes the lariat. U1 marks the 5′ splice site and U2 marks the branch point. The exons are then joined.

8. What is alternative splicing?

One primary transcript can yield more than one mature mRNA, for example by skipping an exon. That is a source of protein diversity and of disease when a splice site is mutated.

9. Reverse transcriptase differs from RNA polymerase because it

Reverse transcriptase writes DNA from an RNA template and, unlike RNA polymerase, requires a primer such as oligo(dT) or a random hexamer.

10. A run that starts with RNA, makes cDNA, and then amplifies that cDNA is called

RT-PCR means reverse transcription followed by PCR. qPCR only describes real-time detection. Doing both is RT-qPCR. A Southern blot starts from DNA and does not amplify it this way.

Where this sits

Both figures are original schematics. Promoters, the three nuclear polymerases, the cap, the spliceosome, and polyadenylation follow the account in Alberts and colleagues, Molecular Biology of the Cell. The clinical reading of RT-PCR versus real-time PCR follows Buckingham, Molecular Diagnostics. Polymerase product lists are the standard board assignments, including the two exceptions worth memorizing: 5S rRNA and U6 snRNA are RNA polymerase III products.

item.title: Plasmid detection versus reconstruction from short reads
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
If you care about mobile antimicrobial resistance, you eventually meet a practical genomics problem: the plasmid is real, the short-read assembly is broken into pieces, and the software has to guess which pieces belong together. A 2025 Briefings in Bioinformatics benchmark by Teixeira and colleagues puts that problem under a bright light across many species, not only E. coli (doi:10.1093/bib/bbaf589).

This lesson turns their main ideas into teaching language you can reuse when reading plasmid papers or choosing a tool for a short-read project.

NoteScope

Educational walkthrough of concepts from Teixeira et al., Brief Bioinform 2025;26(6):bbaf589. Not a substitute for reading the paper or a software manual.

Two jobs that people often mash together

Plasmid detection asks: is this contig from a plasmid or from the chromosome?

Plasmid reconstruction (contig binning) asks: which plasmid contigs belong to the same plasmid molecule?

Detection can look strong while reconstruction still fails. That split is the first concept worth keeping separate in your notes.

Why short reads make this hard Repeats and insertion sequences shared with the chromosome or other plasmids break assemblies. Mosaic plasmids also drift away from database references. Long reads help, but most public assemblies are still short-read only, so the problem remains central for AMR surveillance.

What the benchmark actually compared

The authors built hybrid long-plus-short assemblies as ground truth for 250 genomes spanning Enterobacterales and Enterococcus, then fed short-read-only assemblies into tools. That design matters: without an independent truth set, tool rankings become circular.

They scored detection with precision, recall, and F1. They scored reconstruction with clustering metrics: homogeneity (bin purity), completeness (whether a plasmid was split), and normalized mutual information (NMI).

Top detection performers in their hands included Plasmer, PlasmidEC, PlaScope, and gplas2. For reconstruction, gplas2 led, yet fewer than half of plasmids were perfectly reconstructed. That single sentence should calm anyone who treats a binning output as finished biology.

Database representation and contig length/contiguity drove detection quality. Enterobacterales plasmids, better mirrored in PLSDB-style resources, were easier to spot than many novel enterococcal plasmids.

Assembly fragmentation and having more plasmids made binning harder. Even the best tool left many plasmids incomplete or contaminated. Contiguity is not a luxury setting; it is part of the scientific result.

ARG-carrying plasmids were often more fragmented and harder to reconstruct. Some detection tools also struggled more with ARG contigs, partly because mobile elements around resistance genes break assemblies into short pieces.

The teaching point for modelers and microbiologists

This paper sits next to our earlier genetics notes for a reason. In chromosome versus plasmid resistance and HGT and MIC ecology, plasmids change how fast MIC ecology can move. Teixeira et al. add the bioinformatics warning: if your short-read pipeline cannot reliably say which ARG sits on which plasmid, your downstream story about mobility is partly invented.

A practical habit after reading their results:

  1. Report whether you did detection only or full reconstruction.
  2. Say how contiguous the assembly was.
  3. Note whether the taxon is well represented in plasmid databases.
  4. Treat perfect plasmid circles from short reads as uncommon, especially for large ARG plasmids.
  5. Prefer hybrid or long-read confirmation when a specific plasmid linkage is the claim that matters.

How to talk about tools without hero worship

Different tools use databases, marker genes, machine learning, or assembly-graph topology. The benchmark shows several strategies can detect well. Reconstruction remains the harder hill. Choosing one fashionable package is less important than matching the tool to your taxon, your assembly quality, and whether your scientific question needs contig labels or true plasmid bins.

Takeaway

Detection asks “plasmid or not?” Reconstruction asks “which pieces are one plasmid?” Database bias and broken assemblies still decide much of the outcome. For AMR work, that means plasmid claims from short-read drafts need humility, especially when resistance genes ride fragmented mobile DNA.

Source: Teixeira M, et al. Circling in on plasmids. Briefings in Bioinformatics 2025;26(6):bbaf589. https://doi.org/10.1093/bib/bbaf589

item.title: Mini case: putting CAZ-AVI style PK/PD together
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
This lesson stitches the earlier notes into one worked story. The drug pair is ceftazidime-avibactam style thinking: a beta-lactam plus a protector. The goal is not to deliver a clinical dose recommendation. The goal is to show how a careful modeler moves from fragmented evidence to a joint attainment question without laundering uncertainty.

NoteScope

Teaching case for method order and joint logic. Numbers here are illustrative shapes, not a substitute for a full evidence-composite package.

The question in one sentence

In critically ill adults without renal replacement therapy, given a continuous-infusion style regimen, how often do virtual subjects jointly clear a free ceftazidime exposure rule against MIC and an avibactam threshold rule?

Notice what that sentence already fixed: population, infusion idea, free-drug thinking, and joint success.

Step 1: keep the components separate

Ceftazidime and avibactam get their own concentration-time profiles. Binding, clearance, and variability are component-specific. If published clearances are correlated, that correlation belongs in the draw. Collapsing both drugs into one fake “combo level” throws away the reason the pair exists.

Why joint logic appears here A subject can pass the beta-lactam rule and fail the inhibitor rule. Counting that subject as a success would answer a different question than combination adequacy.

Step 2: choose targets you can defend

A common teaching pattern is:

  • ceftazidime judged on a free steady-state concentration relative to MIC,
  • avibactam judged on staying above a fixed free threshold,
  • joint success only when both pass.

Whatever thresholds you use, cite them and keep free/total conversion explicit.

Step 3: put kidney function in the population

Continuous infusion steady levels move with clearance. eGFR strata are not optional decoration for this story. Draw or assign renal classes, map them to clearance, and report attainment by stratum as well as overall. If the labeled regimen adjusts by renal function, say whether you modeled that adjustment.

Step 4: build PTA, then maybe CFR

Compute joint PTA across an MIC grid for the beta-lactam rule while the inhibitor rule stays active in every subject. If you have a dated MIC distribution for the relevant Gram-negative ecology, weight the PTA curve to get joint CFR. Then re-run under an alternate MIC prior if plasmid-driven shifts are a live concern.

Evidence labels → component PK → free conversion → joint target rule → renal strata → Monte Carlo → joint PTA grid → optional CFR → sensitivity on fu, correlation, and MIC prior.

Do not skip provenance for donor PK pieces, free/total bookkeeping, joint intersection logic, or a plain-language scenario compatibility note.

Step 5: say what the case did not claim

A plasma free-drug joint PTA is not automatically ELF adequacy. A standard-inoculum MIC grid is not automatically a high-burden abscess story. Healthy-volunteer donor pieces are not automatically ICU truth. Write those limits in ordinary sentences. Readers forgive uncertainty. They distrust invisible upgrades.

Closing checklist you can read aloud

  1. Are both components simulated, with free/total stated?
  2. Is success defined as an intersection, not an average?
  3. Are eGFR strata in the population, with dosing rules named?
  4. Are donor PK and MIC sources labeled and dated?
  5. Did you show joint PTA across MIC, and CFR only under an explicit ecology prior?
  6. Did you name what you did not model: effect site, inoculum, RRT, and so on?

If you can answer those six without flipping through hidden notes, the teaching case did its job. A full research package will add more calibration and sensitivity detail, but the skeleton stays the same.

Takeaway

The CAZ-AVI style case is a checklist in narrative form: separate components, free-drug honesty, joint intersection, renal structure, provenance, then PTA/CFR. If you can explain those choices out loud without slides, the simulation is ready to be read by another scientist.

Related lessons: Joint targets, Free drug, eGFR strata, Provenance. Project page: CAZ-AVI evidence-composite PK/PD.

item.title: Inoculum effect: when bacterial density changes the drug story
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Lab MIC work usually starts with a standardized inoculum. Infections do not always politely match that density. In some drug-bug pairs, a denser starting population makes the antibiotic look less effective. That pattern is called the inoculum effect.

For modelers, the point is not to memorize every organism that shows it. The point is to stop treating “the MIC” as independent from bacterial burden when the literature says otherwise.

NoteScope

Conceptual warning for PD inputs and scenario design. Not a complete microbiology review of every inoculum-sensitive pair.

What people mean by inoculum effect

In plain terms: the same drug may need a higher concentration, or may kill more slowly, when the starting bacterial count is much higher. Enzymes can be more abundant. Binding or local drug depletion can matter more. Quorum-related physiology can change. The assay MIC at standard inoculum can then understate the challenge of a high-burden infection.

That does not mean every PTA grid is wrong. It means a high-inoculum pneumonia, endocarditis vegetation, or undrained focus may deserve a harsher PD scenario than a bloodstream model with lower density.

A modeling translation Inoculum effect can appear as a higher effective MIC, a shifted PD curve, or slower kill parameters at high CFU. Pick the representation that matches your data, and label the inoculum assumption.

Same drug, denser start, harder climb to the same effect.

Where this collides with PTA habits

Classic PTA uses an MIC distribution from standard testing. If your clinical question is a high-burden site with a known inoculum effect for that class, a second scenario with worsened PD inputs is more honest than a single optimistic curve.

This also connects to tolerance and persistence. High density can change early kill even when categorical susceptibility looks unchanged. Keep the mechanism language careful: inoculum effect is not automatically “resistance,” though both can raise the practical exposure need.

Acceptable when literature for that drug-bug pair shows little inoculum dependence, or when you clearly limit the claim to standard-assay MIC targets.

Run a base MIC/PTA case, then a high-inoculum case with cited PD worsening. Compare both. Do not average them into one unexplained hybrid.

Practical reporting

State the inoculum assumed by your PD target. If you borrowed in vitro high-inoculum data, mark them as donor evidence and check scenario compatibility. High-inoculum lab conditions are not automatically the same as an ICU pneumonia densitiy, but they are often closer to the worry you are trying to name.

How to keep the wording clean

Say “high-inoculum scenario” when you worsened PD inputs based on cited in vitro density effects. Do not say “resistant” unless genetics or MIC category actually changed. Do not say “persistent” unless you modeled a refractory subpopulation. Inoculum effect can interact with those ideas, but the labels should stay separate so collaborators know which lever you moved.

If the literature for your drug-bug pair is thin, it is better to list inoculum as an unquantified limitation than to invent a severity factor with no source. Empty honesty beats decorative precision.

Takeaway

Bacterial density can change the pharmacodynamic hill the drug must climb. When the literature flags an inoculum effect, put density into the scenario list beside MIC, binding, and renal function. Otherwise your clean PTA may describe a lighter fight than the infection.

item.title: Renal function and eGFR strata in antibiotic PK/PD
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Many antibiotics leave the body through the kidney. When clearance depends on renal function, two patients on the “same” regimen can live in different exposure worlds. One has high free levels and long time above MIC. Another clears the drug so fast the troughs collapse.

That is why serious virtual populations often stratify by eGFR or similar kidney metrics instead of pretending one clearance distribution fits everybody.

NoteScope

Modeling structure for renally cleared drugs. Not individualized clinical dosing advice.

Why kidney function changes the plot

If clearance rises as eGFR rises, the concentration-time curve sits lower for better renal function, all else equal. For time-driven targets, that can erase trough coverage first. For continuous infusion, steady free concentration moves almost directly with clearance. For AUC-driven targets, the whole area shrinks.

So renal strata are not decorative subgroups. They are different pharmacokinetic machines.

Better kidney function can mean less exposure on the same nominal regimen.

Augmented renal clearance Some critically ill patients clear drugs unusually fast. If your virtual population never includes that tail, PTA for “ICU adults” can look calmer than the ward you claim to study.

Building strata without clutter

A practical pattern:

  1. Define eGFR classes that match the covariate model you cite.
  2. Draw subjects inside each class, or draw eGFR then map to clearance.
  3. Report PTA within strata and overall.
  4. Keep dosing rules explicit if the labeled regimen itself adjusts by kidney function.

If the clinical regimen reduces dose in low eGFR, your simulation should not compare “full dose in everyone” unless that is the deliberate what-if.

Useful for understanding raw pharmacokinetic sensitivity to kidney function. Can overstate exposure in low eGFR and understate risk in high eGFR relative to labeled practice.

Closer to practice questions. Each stratum gets its regimen rule, then PTA is compared under those rules. Still cite which adjustment scheme you implemented.

What to report so readers can trust you

Name the equation used for renal function, the class boundaries, the clearance relationship, and whether dialysis or renal replacement scenarios were excluded. Mixed populations without labels are hard to reuse and easy to over-interpret.

What changes in the figure when you stratify

Overall PTA can hide a split world: strong attainment in low eGFR and fragile attainment in high eGFR on the same nominal dose. Or the reverse after renal dose reductions that overshoot. Stratified plots make that visible. A single pooled PTA can average the tension away.

When you present, show at least one stratum contrast beside the overall number. Readers who treat ICU kidneys as one bin will misuse your result. Readers who see the bins can argue with you productively about class boundaries and clearance equations.

If renal replacement therapy is excluded, say that in the first methods paragraph. Mixed RRT and non-RRT evidence is a classic provenance trap.

Also write down which equation produced eGFR or creatinine clearance in your covariate chain. Switching formulas mid-project is a quiet way to invent a new population without noticing.

If body size and renal function both enter clearance, keep that structure intact in the virtual draws. Dropping weight while keeping eGFR, or the reverse, can warp the tails that decide PTA at higher MIC values.

Takeaway

For renally cleared antibiotics, eGFR is not a demographic decoration. It reshapes clearance, exposure geometry, and attainment. Put kidney function into the virtual population on purpose, then say whether dosing was fixed or adjusted.

item.title: Effect site versus plasma: where the bug actually lives
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Most antibiotic PK models begin in plasma because plasma is what we can sample often. Many infections, though, are not happening in a blood vial. Pneumonia asks about lung concentrations. Meningitis asks about CSF. Abscesses and bone infections have their own stubborn geography.

This lesson is about the gap between what we measure and where the bacteria sit, and how to keep that gap from becoming an invisible leap of faith.

NoteScope

Modeling intuition about site of infection. Not a catalog of tissue penetration coefficients for every drug.

Plasma is a proxy, sometimes a good one

If free plasma exposure tracks free exposure at the effect site closely enough for your question, plasma-based PTA can be a fair first tool. If the site is protected, poorly perfused, or governed by transporters, plasma can flatter the regimen.

A simple mental split helps:

  • Plasma-centric question: given systemic PK, how often do we clear a plasma free-drug target?
  • Site-aware question: given systemic PK plus a site model or site observations, how often does the effect-site exposure clear the relevant target?

Those are different claims. Both can be useful. They should not share one sentence in the abstract as if they were identical.

A sentence worth refusing “Plasma fT>MIC was high, therefore lung exposure was adequate.” That “therefore” needs evidence about penetration, timing, and free fraction at the site.

A site curve can be lower, delayed, or both. Plasma success does not automatically copy over.

Common site stories modelers meet

Epithelial lining fluid (ELF) for pneumonia work: ratios to plasma vary by drug and sampling time.
CSF for meningitis: barrier and inflammation change penetration.
Tissue or abscess: averages may hide necrotic cores where drug arrives late.

In each case you need either direct site observations, a justified transfer model, or an honest plasma-only limitation statement.

Defensible when you clearly claim a plasma free-drug endpoint. Weak when the abstract quietly upgrades that claim into site adequacy.

Apply a published penetration ratio or time-varying factor, cite it, and sensitivity-test lower ratios. Keep free/total bookkeeping intact at the site if data allow.

Best case: measured site concentrations with timing. Still watch assay method, inflammation state, and whether samples represent the infected subcompartment.

How to write this without hand-waving

In methods, name the compartment your target refers to. In limitations, say what you did not model. If donor ELF or CSF data come from a different population than your primary PK, treat them with the same provenance care you would use for a borrowed clearance equation.

Two abstracts, only one is honest

Honest: “We evaluated free plasma target attainment for regimen X in a virtual ICU population. Site-of-infection concentrations were not modeled.”

Overstated: “We showed regimen X provides adequate lung exposure,” after only plasma PTA.

The first abstract can still be scientifically valuable. The second asks readers to invent a penetration model you never wrote down. If you do have ELF or CSF data, bring them in with dates, methods, and sensitivity to lower penetration. If you do not, keep the claim inside plasma and sleep better.

Timing matters too. A site-to-plasma ratio from a late sampling window may not describe early therapy. If your PTA question includes the first hours, a single steady ratio can be the wrong proxy.

Takeaway

Bacteria live at an effect site. Plasma is often the ladder we climb to estimate that site, not the destination itself. Keep the proxy relationship visible, or your PTA will answer a cleaner question than the infection deserves.

item.title: Horizontal gene transfer and MIC ecology
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is sideways inheritance: genes moving between bacteria that are not simply parent and child. Plasmids, transposons, and related elements do a lot of that traffic for resistance.

For PK/PD, you rarely need the full molecular soap opera. You need one consequence: MIC distributions can change faster than a stable chromosomal lineage would suggest. CFR depends on those distributions. So HGT is an aging clock on your epidemiology prior.

NoteScope

Genetics as annotation on the MIC layer used by PTA/CFR.

From gene traffic to P(MIC)

CFR needs weights: how common is each MIC category in the population you care about? That is an ecological claim. It includes species, region, year, specimen mix, and which mechanisms are circulating.

If a plasmid carrying a clinically important enzyme expands in a hospital network, the right-hand side of the MIC histogram can fatten within seasons. A CFR computed on last year’s weights can remain numerically tidy and scientifically late.

What HGT does not do HGT does not replace pharmacometrics. Clearance, infusion mode, and free-drug targets still matter. HGT tells you when the MIC weights under those calculations need a fresh date stamp.

Habits that survive contact with mobile resistance

  1. Date-stamp every MIC source used in CFR.
  2. Separate mechanism strata when the data allow (enzyme class versus target mutation).
  3. Recompute CFR under alternate local distributions as sensitivity analysis.
  4. Avoid promoting one ward antibiogram into a universal prior.
  5. Keep the chromosome-versus-plasmid distinction nearby when you talk about stability.

Chromosomal lineage-dominant resistance, slow local change, consistent species mix, recent surveillance with clear methods.

Known plasmid outbreak potential, rapid MIC shifts in neighboring centers, mixed specimen sources, or an old surveillance table reused without comment.

A concrete CFR story

Your PTA curve looks reassuring through MIC 4 mg/L and then falls. Under last year’s local distribution, most isolates sit at MIC 1 or 2, so CFR looks high. This year a plasmid-associated enzyme becomes common and the mass shifts toward MIC 4 and 8. The PTA curve did not change. CFR did, because the weights changed.

That is why dating the MIC prior is not bureaucracy. It is part of naming the ecological world your summary number lives in. If you only have an old table, say so and show a harsher alternate prior beside it.

Pair this habit with the chromosome-versus-plasmid lesson: mobility tells you how nervous to be about calendar age.

When surveillance is sparse, you can still be useful. Report PTA as the main figure and treat CFR as exploratory under two or three stated priors. That is better than one confident CFR built on an undated convenience sample.

Ask the microbiology lab what changed recently: outbreak notes, new carbapenemase detections, or shifted species mix. Informal context is not a substitute for surveillance tables, but it tells you whether yesterday’s prior deserves extra suspicion.

Takeaway

Treat MIC ecology as perishable when mobile elements are in play. Your PTA curve can stay the same while CFR moves, simply because the weights under the curve changed.

item.title: Uncertainty and provenance in PK/PD evidence
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
A smooth PTA curve can look like certainty. Often it is a stack of borrowed numbers wearing a clean plot. The scientific job is not only to compute a probability. It is to show which assumptions, from which sources, under which scenario rules, produced that probability.

This lesson is about evidence hygiene. It is the difference between a reusable simulation and a one-off slide.

NoteScope

Provenance habits for antimicrobial PK/PD simulation, aligned with component-level evidence thinking.

Label every input like it might be audited

Useful labels look boring. That is why they work.

Label Meaning
Directly reported Used as published for this purpose
Transformed Unit change, free/total conversion, algebra
Donor / inherited Borrowed from a related but non-identical source
Assumed Filled so the model can run; must stay visible
Scenario-generated Created by the simulation design itself

Missing data should stay missing until a compatible donor is justified. Silent median fills create false completeness.

A practical test If a coauthor asks “where did this fu come from?” and you need five minutes to remember, the provenance trail is already too weak for a methods section.

Uncertainty comes in layers

  1. Parameter uncertainty: IIV, residual error, covariate effects.
  2. Structural uncertainty: compartment choice, infusion constraints, correlation.
  3. Evidence uncertainty: wrong population, wrong matrix, stale MIC ecology.
  4. Decision-rule uncertainty: which threshold counts as “enough.”

Monte Carlo on layer 1 alone can look precise while layer 3 quietly dominates.

Pretty sampling does not repair a shaky evidence base.

Source list for CL, V, fu, targets, MIC weights. Free/total notes. Population statement. Seed and N. One sensitivity check on the most fragile input.

Everything in the minimum set, plus scenario compatibility notes for donor evidence, correlation assumptions, convergence checks, and alternative MIC priors with dates.

Compatibility is a scientific decision

ICU continuous-infusion parameters are not automatically interchangeable with healthy-volunteer bolus data, CSF studies, or in vitro kill curves. Those sources can still help as donors or anchors. They should not be pooled as if they were one population. Write the compatibility rule in human language: what was allowed to enter the primary scenario, and what stayed outside with a label.

What good provenance feels like in a meeting

Someone asks why ICU PTA used a clearance relationship from a continuous-infusion critically ill study and an MIC table from a regional surveillance year. You can answer in one breath: primary PK from source A for scenario match, MIC weights from source B dated to that year, fu transformed from total using source C, inhibitor threshold from source D with a compatibility note. No scavenger hunt through forgotten spreadsheets.

If you cannot give that breath-length answer, stop polishing the figure and rebuild the input table first. Most “mysterious” PTA sensitivity traces back to one unlabeled donor.

Keep a one-page input ledger beside the code: parameter, value or distribution, source, transformation, scenario role. It is unglamorous. It is also what makes the project reusable six months later.

Takeaway

Reproducible PK/PD is less about fancier random draws and more about refusing to launder uncertain evidence into false certainty. If the trail of sources is clear, other people can challenge your result productively. That is a feature.

item.title: Joint targets for beta-lactam / beta-lactamase inhibitor pairs
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
A beta-lactam paired with a beta-lactamase inhibitor is not one medicine with a long name. One partner usually does the killing work. The other protects that work from enzymes. If protection fails, the beta-lactam can look adequate on a plot and still lose in the patient.

That is why combination PK/PD often needs a joint rule: both conditions true in the same virtual subject at the same evaluation window.

NoteScope

Simulation logic for combinations, with ceftazidime-avibactam style problems as a teaching frame. Not product-specific clinical advice.

Two conditions, one success flag

Suppose drug A must meet a free-exposure target against MIC, and drug B must stay above a threshold that preserves A’s activity. For each simulated person:

[ = {A} {B} ]

Joint PTA is the fraction of people for whom that intersection is true. It is not the average of PTA(A) and PTA(B). It is not “A looks fine, so ignore B.”

Why correlation between clearances matters If A and B clearances move together, the joint tail can be very different from two independent draws. Ignoring correlation can make joint failure look rarer or more common than your evidence supports. State the correlation assumption.

Mistakes that look sophisticated

  1. Simulating only the beta-lactam because “that is the antibiotic.”
  2. Reporting the mean of two PTAs as if it were joint attainment.
  3. Borrowing an inhibitor threshold from another matrix or population without labeling.
  4. Collapsing both drugs into one fake combined concentration.

Simulate free concentration-time for A and for B in each virtual subject. Keep units and binding honest for each component.

Apply each target. Mark success only when both pass. Build PTA versus MIC from that joint indicator. Optionally weight by MIC ecology for joint CFR.

Average(PTA_A, PTA_B), or "A passed so count success." Those shortcuts answer different questions and can hide inhibitor-limited regimens.

Why this shows up in CAZ-AVI style work

Ceftazidime and avibactam are a teaching example because the beta-lactam exposure and the inhibitor exposure are not interchangeable. A regimen can clear a ceftazidime rule while avibactam is the limiting partner, or the reverse depending on the scenario. Component-level evidence reconstruction exists partly because papers report pieces of that system separately, and the modeler has to keep those pieces labeled until a joint rule is applied on purpose.

A tiny counting example

Imagine 100 virtual subjects.

  • 90 pass the beta-lactam rule.
  • 80 pass the inhibitor rule.
  • Only 70 pass both.

Joint PTA is 70%. The average of 90% and 80% is 85%. That 15-point gap is exactly why intersection logic exists. If clearances are positively correlated, joint failures may cluster; if not, the overlap changes again. Either way, report the joint indicator you actually coded.

When you write results, show component PTA only as supporting context. Lead with joint PTA if the clinical object is the combination.

If you need a debugging view, plot the fraction failing A only, B only, and both. That split tells you whether the regimen is beta-lactam limited, inhibitor limited, or jointly fragile. A single joint number hides that diagnosis.

Takeaway

For BL/BLI pairs, protection failure is regimen failure. Joint PTA is an intersection inside each simulated person. Build it that way, then be transparent about thresholds, correlation, and which MIC the beta-lactam rule refers to.

item.title: Intermittent vs continuous infusion for beta-lactams
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
For many beta-lactams the index that matters most is time above a threshold. That makes how you deliver the dose part of the pharmacology, not a nursing footnote.

Give the same daily amount as short intermittent infusions and you get peaks and troughs. Stretch the infusion and the troughs rise. Run it continuously and the profile can settle toward a steady free concentration. The MIC line does not move. The geometry around it does.

NoteScope

Geometry of infusion mode for simulation. Not a recommendation to change bedside practice by itself.

Same daily dose, different shape

Hold clearance, volume, fu, and MIC fixed. Change only the input rate.

  • Intermittent short infusion: oscillating free levels. Success depends on how long each cycle stays above MIC.
  • Extended infusion: softer peaks, higher troughs.
  • Continuous infusion: approach to steady state. Many analyses then ask whether steady free concentration stays above MIC, or above a multiple of MIC.

Infusion mode changes which parts of the day sit above the MIC line.

Why loading doses appear in continuous regimens If you start continuous infusion with no load, early concentrations climb slowly. A PTA that only looks at later steady state can miss early undershoot. If your clinical question includes the first hours, model the load.

What the simulator must keep honest

  1. Loading dose status.
  2. Renal function strata, because steady concentration moves with clearance.
  3. Administration constraints that your scenario ignores (stability, line access). Label them.
  4. Target form: percent fT>MIC versus a Css/MIC ratio rule. They are related ideas with different bookkeeping.

Freeze the virtual population and MIC grid. Change only the dosing input. Plot PTA on the same MIC axis. Report early and steady periods if loading differs.

Changing infusion mode and also silently changing daily dose, population, or target definition. Then attributing the whole PTA jump to "continuous infusion magic."

A classroom example without fake precision

Suppose two regimens deliver the same daily free-drug amount, one as intermittent doses and one as continuous infusion after a load. At low MIC both may look fine. As MIC rises, the intermittent troughs fail first while continuous Css may still clear a Css/MIC rule. That pattern is exactly why people study infusion mode. It is also why you must keep daily dose and population fixed when you make the comparison.

How to talk about this without overselling

A fair sentence sounds like this: “Under the same daily dose and the same virtual population, continuous infusion improved PTA at higher MIC values because trough undershoot disappeared; early coverage still depended on the loading dose.”

An unfair sentence sounds like this: “Continuous infusion is better,” with no fixed daily dose, no population lock, and no target definition.

Also remember pharmacy and line realities. A simulation can assume perfect continuous delivery. A ward may not. If your scenario ignores stability windows or access constraints, write that limitation in ordinary language. The PK/PD geometry lesson remains useful either way.

One more practical tip: when two papers disagree about continuous infusion benefit, check whether they locked daily dose, population, free/total handling, and target definition. Many apparent contradictions dissolve once those four locks are compared side by side.

Takeaway

Infusion mode redraws the exposure path around the MIC. For time-driven beta-lactam targets, that redraw is part of the science. Compare shapes under controlled conditions, and say whether your endpoint was interval fT>MIC or steady-state coverage.

item.title: Free drug and protein binding
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Open a PK/PD paper and you will often see a little f in front of the target: fT>MIC, fAUC/MIC. That letter is easy to skim past. It is also where many simulations go wrong.

Most antibacterial targets are written for free (unbound) drug. Many concentration models are fitted to total plasma levels. If you compare total curves to free targets, the regimen looks stronger than the rule you claimed to test.

NoteScope

Unit hygiene for exposure-effect work. Not a dosing calculator.

What free means in plain language

In plasma, some drug molecules stick to proteins such as albumin. The usual modeling story says the unbound molecules are the ones available to act. The MIC assay is generally interpreted on that unbound-compatible scale. So the simulator should put free concentration versus time next to MIC.

A simple linear correction is:

[ C_{}(t)=f_uC_{}(t) ]

where (f_u) is the unbound fraction. This is a starting point, not a religion. Binding can change with albumin, pregnancy, burns, or critical illness. For a highly bound drug, a small error in (f_u) becomes a large error in free exposure.

A numbers intuition If fu = 0.2, only one fifth of the total concentration counts toward a free-drug target. Using the total curve unchanged is like pretending there is five times more active drug than your target definition allows.

The free curve is the one that should meet a free-drug MIC rule.

Where people get hurt in practice

  1. Target says free, plotted series is total.
  2. fu comes from healthy volunteers, applied unchanged to hypoalbuminemic ICU patients.
  3. The infection is not in plasma (ELF, CSF, tissue), but the model never leaves the plasma compartment.
  4. Combination regimens use one fu for both components without checking.

Model outputs total concentration, multiplies by a cited fu, then tests 100% fT>MIC. The methods line states free/total conversion and the fu source.

Model outputs total concentration and directly counts time above MIC using a free-drug target wording. PTA looks great. The claim is overstated by roughly the binding factor.

A short checklist before you run PTA

  • Label every series: free or total.
  • Cite fu and whether it is fixed, sampled, or covariate-dependent.
  • Re-run with lower and higher fu as a one-way sensitivity check.
  • For BL/BLI pairs, bind each component on its own terms.
  • If the effect site is not plasma, say so and move to the effect-site lesson with honest humility.

Walk through one messy case

You fit a model to total plasma concentrations. The target you want is 100% fT>MIC. Literature fu is 0.25 in healthy volunteers, but your population is critically ill and often hypoalbuminemic. A first run uses fu = 0.25. A second run uses fu = 0.40 as a what-if for lower binding. A third run keeps total concentrations and “forgets” the f, which wrongly inflates attainment.

Only the first two runs belong in a serious report, and both should be shown if binding is uncertain. The third run is a unit error dressed as optimism.

When you present results, say the free/total conversion out loud before you show the PTA plot. If listeners cannot tell whether the curve is free or total, the figure is not ready.

Takeaway

Binding is not cosmetic formatting. It decides which curve is allowed to talk to the MIC. Align the binding state of the PK output with the binding state of the PD target before you interpret attainment.

item.title: Chromosome vs plasmid resistance for PK/PD modelers
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
PK/PD models usually do not simulate DNA base by base. They simulate exposure and a phenotype, often an MIC. Genetics still belongs in the room, because it tells you how stable that phenotype is and how fast the local MIC ecology can shift.

This lesson is a bridge for modelers. Enough bacterial genetics to stop treating every MIC cell in a table as the same kind of object.

NoteScope

Genetics for people who build exposure-response simulations. Not a full genomics course.

Two homes for resistance genes

Resistance can live on the chromosome or on a plasmid (and related mobile elements). Both can raise an MIC. They do not raise it with the same epidemiological behavior.

Chromosomal changes often travel mostly with the lineage: mother cell to daughter cell. Plasmid-borne resistance can move horizontally as well, sometimes across lineages or species. Plasmid copy number can also amplify expression, so “same gene” is not always “same burden.”

Feature Chromosomal Plasmid-borne, typical case
Main inheritance Vertical Vertical and often horizontal
Dose / copy effect Usually limited copies Copy number can boost expression
Speed of ecological change Often slower within a hospital Can surge when a plasmid expands
Modeling note Phenotype may be more lineage-stable MIC priors may age faster
Why this matters for CFR CFR needs P(MIC). If that distribution is shaped by a spreading plasmid, last year’s weights can quietly expire. Date-stamp the source and, when possible, separate mechanism strata.

Same MIC number, different story

Imagine two isolates with MIC = 8 mg/L to the same drug.

In isolate A, a chromosomal target mutation reduced binding. In isolate B, a plasmid beta-lactamase is chewing the drug. A PTA grid may treat them identically if it only sees “8”. A combination with an inhibitor may help B and do little for A. Your joint-target lesson later depends on knowing which world you are in.

What to change in a PK/PD workflow

  1. Label MIC provenance with date, region, species, and method.
  2. Ask whether the mechanism is enzyme-mediated before you lean on inhibitor partners.
  3. Refresh local MIC weights more aggressively when plasmid epidemics are active.
  4. Keep genetics in the annotation layer unless you are explicitly building a genotype-to-phenotype model.

Expect more stability inside a clonal background, but still verify species ID and assay method. Target mutations may need a different therapeutic logic than enzyme blockade.

Expect mobility, possible copy-number effects, and faster change in hospital ecology. CFR priors deserve dates and sensitivity checks.

A short example conversation

Someone hands you an MIC table and asks for CFR. Before you run anything, ask three genetics-aware questions:

  1. Are these isolates dominated by one clone, or is the lab seeing mixed plasmid traffic?
  2. How old is the table, and has the hospital seen a recent enzyme-gene surge?
  3. If we later evaluate an inhibitor combination, does the mechanism even match that idea?

You may still proceed with a standard CFR. The difference is that your methods paragraph will say what kind of phenotype ecology you assumed, instead of pretending every MIC cell is interchangeable biology.

If the answer to those questions is “we do not know,” that is still useful. Unknown mobility is itself a reason to run sensitivity CFR under a harsher MIC prior.

Takeaway

Do not ask genetics to replace PK/PD. Ask it to annotate the MIC layer: how mobile is this phenotype, how old is the ecology prior, and which mechanism your target rule quietly assumes?

item.title: Resistance, tolerance, and persistence in PK/PD language
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
In everyday talk, if an antibiotic fails people often say the bug was resistant. That shorthand is understandable. It is also expensive for modeling, because it points the simulator at the wrong object.

This lesson separates three survival ideas and translates them into what a PK/PD model can see: a moved threshold, a slower kill, or a long surviving tail.

NoteScope

Concept map for simulation and reading papers. Related preprint context: comparative modeling of resistance, tolerance, and persistence.

Three words that should not be synonyms

Resistance usually means a heritable drop in susceptibility. In practice that often shows up as a higher MIC or a shifted pharmacodynamic curve. Genetics can sit underneath (target mutation, enzyme, efflux), but the PK/PD layer mainly notices the phenotype change.

Tolerance means a population can endure drug pressure longer without a large MIC shift. Time-kill curves look sluggish. The organism is not “fully susceptible in behavior” just because the MIC table looks polite.

Persistence points to a small subpopulation that survives much longer. The bulk may fall, then a refractory tail remains. Relapse risk lives in that tail more than in the first steep decline.

Idea What moved What a model needs
Resistance Threshold / MIC Updated MIC or PD curve
Tolerance Kill speed of the population Time-kill or slower kill-rate terms
Persistence Long-lived fraction Biphasic kill or persister compartment
A quick self-check If changing the MIC fully explains the failure story, you are mostly in resistance territory. If MIC barely moved but killing stalled, look at tolerance or persistence before you keep tuning the dose in a PTA-only frame.

What the curves look like

Same starting inoculum, different survival stories. MIC alone may not separate these lines.

Why a strong PTA can still disappoint

PTA asks whether exposure clears a threshold rule. That is a fair question. It is not every question.

A regimen can look excellent against the measured MIC distribution while:

  • killing is too slow for the planned duration,
  • a persistent fraction remains,
  • or the assay MIC understates the real challenge at the infection site.

None of that makes PTA useless. It means you should label what your simulation tested. “High PTA vs MIC grid” is not the same claim as “sterilizing cure in every biology.”

Update the MIC distribution or PD curve. Re-run PTA/CFR. Mechanism matters later when you choose inhibitors or drug class switches.

Bring in time-kill information or slower kill parameters. Duration and shape of exposure may matter more than another small dose bump in a MIC-only frame.

Model a refractory fraction or biphasic kill. Ask whether your endpoint is inhibition, bulk kill, or durable clearance of the tail.

Pathogen contrast, briefly

Different organisms lean on different survival styles. In comparative modeling work, Staphylococcus aureus and Mycobacterium tuberculosis are a useful pair: one often shows a faster tolerance-like pattern, the other a longer persistence window. The lesson for the modeler is simple. Do not copy a kill structure from one species into another because the antibiotic name matches.

Takeaway

Resistance moves the threshold. Tolerance slows the population kill. Persistence leaves a long tail. Say which one your simulation is actually testing, especially when the clinical story is failure despite a tidy MIC.

item.title: PTA, CFR, and virtual populations
item.dc:creator: Vahhab Piranfar
item.description:
Once you have an exposure rule and an MIC, a single “typical patient” calculation is rarely enough. Real people differ in clearance, volume, kidney function, and body size. Virtual populations, PTA, and CFR are the tools we use to ask how often a regimen works across that spread.

Think of it as moving from one drawn curve to a cloud of curves, then counting how many of those curves pass the test you chose.

NoteScope

Method intuition for simulation. Not software documentation and not a bedside calculator.

Virtual populations are controlled variation

A virtual population is a set of simulated individuals. For each person you draw pharmacokinetic parameters from distributions that are supposed to reflect interindividual variability. If the literature reports correlated clearances, or clearances that depend on eGFR, that structure belongs in the draw. If you invent tidy independent normals because they look neat, you are no longer studying the published system. You are studying your drawing habits.

Useful discipline looks like this:

  • cite the IIV source,
  • keep covariate rules explicit,
  • record the random seed and the sample size,
  • say which population the parameters came from (ICU, healthy volunteers, dialysis, and so on).
Why sample size shows up in methods sections Too few virtual subjects and the PTA estimate jitters. Extremely large N can look impressive while hiding a bad structural assumption. Report both N and a quick stability check.

PTA: fix the MIC, count the successes

Probability of target attainment (PTA) answers a conditional question:

If MIC equals this value, what fraction of virtual subjects meet the PK/PD target?

You usually compute PTA across a grid of MIC values and plot a declining curve. The interesting part is often the cliff: the MIC region where success falls apart.

PTA is a curve over MIC, not a single trophy number.

CFR: bring the local microbiology back in

Cumulative fraction of response (CFR) folds PTA over an MIC distribution from surveillance or local epidemiology:

[ = _i (_i)P(_i) ]

PTA asks “what if MIC is X?”
CFR asks “given the MICs we actually see around here, how often do we succeed?”

That second question is only as honest as the MIC weights. A distribution from another country, another year, or a mixed species group can make CFR look decisive while answering the wrong question.

Use PTA when you want to see regimen strength across a MIC grid, compare dosing strategies, or find the MIC where performance collapses.

Use CFR when you have a trustworthy local or regional MIC distribution and you want one summary of expected success under that ecology.

Show PTA curves for mechanism insight, then report CFR under one or more dated MIC priors. Sensitivity to the prior is part of the scientific result.

A minimal workflow you can defend

  1. Define regimen and PK model, with provenance.
  2. Define free-drug target or targets.
  3. Simulate N virtual subjects.
  4. Compute PTA on an MIC grid.
  5. Optionally weight by an MIC distribution to get CFR.
  6. Stress-test the fragile inputs: binding, IIV, renal strata, MIC source.

If the target is joint (two drugs, two conditions), success is the intersection inside each virtual subject. Averaging two separate PTA values is not the same thing. A later lesson walks through that case.

Takeaway

Virtual populations turn “does this look fine on paper?” into “how often does this pass under realistic variability?” PTA keeps MIC fixed. CFR brings epidemiology back. Neither repairs a bad target choice or a mismatched population.
